summary: This experimental memo defines a Telnet option that lets a client and server negotiate how to authenticate the user. It was replaced by RFC 1416, which fixed a typo.

eli5.summary: Before letting someone into a remote computer, the computer should check who they are. This paper lets the two sides agree on how to do the checking. A corrected version replaced it.

subtitle: A way for Telnet client and server to agree on how to verify the user's identity

tldr.problem: Telnet users must type their passwords across the network in clear text, vulnerable to eavesdropping if the connection passes through untrusted networks. Remote login needs a secure way to prove identity without exposing passwords.
tldr.mechanism: The AUTHENTICATION option provides a framework for negotiating which authentication system (Kerberos, RSA, SPX, etc.) to use, allowing the client and server to exchange authentication information securely instead of sending passwords in clear text.
tldr.outcome: Systems supporting this option can avoid transmitting passwords in clear text and may automatically send authentication information if the Telnet process has the appropriate credentials. A corrected version, RFC 1416, replaced this RFC due to a typo.

today: RFC 1409 is an experimental protocol replaced by RFC 1416, which corrected a typo in this document. Telnet itself is largely obsolete as a remote login protocol, having been replaced by SSH (Secure Shell) which provides strong encryption and authentication. However, the framework of negotiating authentication methods between client and server established in this RFC influenced the design of later secure remote access protocols.

sections.title: The Security Problem
sections.content:
The Telnet protocol has a significant deficiency: when users log into remote systems, they must type their passwords, which are passed across the network in clear text. If the connection passes through untrusted networks, passwords can be compromised by someone watching the network packets.

The AUTHENTICATION option solves this problem in two ways. First, users' passwords are no longer sent in clear text across the network. Second, if the front-end Telnet process has the appropriate authentication information, it can automatically send the information, and the user will not have to type any password at all.

The AUTHENTICATION option is designed to be general enough to work with any authentication system, whether Kerberos, RSA, SPX, or others. This flexibility allows organizations to choose the authentication mechanism that best fits their security requirements.
sections.eli5: Typing your password over the network is risky because bad people can read it. A better way is to use a secret key that both computers know about, so the password never travels across the network.

sections.title: Authentication Types and Modifiers
sections.content:
The AUTHENTICATION option defines several authentication types that can be used. NULL (type 0) indicates no authentication. Kerberos V4 (type 1) and Kerberos V5 (type 2) use the Kerberos authentication system. SPX (type 3), RSA (type 6), and LOKI (type 10) represent other authentication mechanisms. Additional types can be registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

Each authentication type is paired with a modifier specifying the direction and mode. The AUTH_WHO_MASK bit indicates direction: AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER (0) means the client authenticates to the server, while AUTH_SERVER_TO_CLIENT (1) means the server authenticates to the client.

The AUTH_HOW_MASK bit indicates mode: AUTH_HOW_ONE_WAY (0) is one-way authentication, where only one side proves its identity. AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL (2) is mutual authentication, where both sides prove their identities to each other.

This gives four possible authentication scenarios: client authenticates to server with one-way authentication, server authenticates to client with one-way authentication, client authenticates to server with mutual authentication, or server authenticates to client with mutual authentication (each side then proves itself).
sections.eli5: Different authentication systems (Kerberos, RSA, etc.) can work with Telnet. Each one is paired with a direction (who is proving their identity) and a mode (one way or mutual).

sections.title: Option Negotiation and Commands
sections.content:
The AUTHENTICATION option uses Telnet's standard negotiation commands. The client sends IAC WILL AUTHENTICATION to indicate willingness to send and receive authentication information. The server sends IAC DO AUTHENTICATION to indicate it is willing to send and receive authentication information.

If either side refuses, they send IAC WONT AUTHENTICATION (client) or IAC DONT AUTHENTICATION (server). Authentication negotiation is only performed in one direction: the server must send DO, and the client must send WILL. This removes potential ambiguity.

Once both sides have exchanged DO and WILL, the server is free to request authentication information using IAC SB AUTHENTICATION SEND authentication-type-pair-list IAC SE. The authentication-type-pair-list is an ordered list of authentication-type pairs, with the first type being most preferred and the last being least preferred.

The client responds with IAC SB AUTHENTICATION IS authentication-type-pair <auth data> IAC SE, sending authentication data for one of the types listed by the server. If the client does not support any of the listed types, it responds with NULL to indicate this. The server may send multiple REPLY commands as part of the authentication exchange.

An optional IAC SB AUTHENTICATION NAME remote-user IAC SE command specifies the account name on the remote host that the user wishes to use. Not all authentication mechanisms support this command.
sections.eli5: The client and server first agree to use authentication. The server suggests which authentication methods it likes, in order of preference. The client picks one and sends the required credentials, and they exchange messages until the authentication succeeds or fails.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements and Security
sections.content:
WILL and DO commands are used only at the beginning of the connection to obtain permission for future negotiations. Once permission is granted, the server is the only side allowed to request authentication information via SEND. Only the client may transmit authentication information via IS commands. Only the server may send REPLY commands. As many IS and REPLY suboptions may be exchanged as needed for the particular authentication scheme chosen.

The server MUST order the authentication types offered to indicate preference: first type is most preferred, last type is least preferred. If the client does not support any offered type, it should respond with NULL, but the server may then choose to close the connection.

A critical security implication must be noted: during authentication negotiation, no authentication has yet occurred. Therefore, each system has no way of knowing whether it is talking to the system it intends. An intruder could attempt to negotiate the use of an authentication system that is weak or already compromised. Systems must be designed to mitigate this risk, for example by offering only strong authentication types and refusing to fall back to weaker types.

Every implementation supporting the Telnet AUTHENTICATION option is expected to support the full specification as described in the RFC, including all command types and the ability to exchange multiple authentication suboptions as needed.
sections.eli5: The server suggests and picks which method to use. Both sides exchange messages back and forth, but neither can be sure they are talking to the real other side until authentication is complete. Systems should only offer strong authentication methods.
